introduction: The Founders of religion speak in more than one voice. “I and my Father are one,” says Jesus, and “my Father is greater than I”; “I am only a mortal like you,” says Muḥammad, and the Qur’án says “Allah threw.” The readings explain this by stations. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá names three (the body, the rational soul, and the manifestation of God) and often speaks of two: a human station that eats, sleeps, sorrows and can be despised, and a divine one that is like the sun in a spotless mirror. The mirror has no light of its own, and that is why Bahá’u’lláh can say that when he speaks of divinity he means his “complete and absolute self-effacement.” The Gospel sayings of both kinds are set side by side here, with Paul, the Letter to the Hebrews and the Qur’án’s verses on the mortal Messenger. Three traditions press on the readings from different sides: the Nicene Creed, which says more than “manifestation”; the Qur’án and Guru Gobind Singh, who forbid calling any messenger God; and Ḥalláj and the Upanishads, who find divinity in the self.
questions: “I and my Father are one” and “my Father is greater than I.” How does the idea of stations let both stand? Is anything left unexplained?
“Divinity, whenever I mention it, indicateth My complete and absolute self-effacement.” Why would a claim to divinity be the opposite of a claim for oneself? Use the image of the mirror.

The Nicene Creed says “of one substance with the Father”; the readings say the sun appears in the mirror without descending into it. What is the practical difference for worship and for relations with other religions?
The Qur’án condemns those who say God is the Messiah. How would you explain “verily I am God!” in the third reading to a Muslim friend?
The human station is called a veil. Why would God make recognition depend on seeing past a carpenter, an unlettered merchant, a prisoner?
‘Abdu’l-Bahá says man has the same two conditions as Christ. What is shared between a Manifestation and any human being, and what is not?

outside.why: Looking at his own self, he “findeth it the most insignificant of all creation.” Jesus: I can of mine own self do nothing.
Looking at what he has been empowered to manifest, “that self is transfigured.” Jesus: I and my Father are one.
“Divinity, whenever I mention it, indicateth My complete and absolute self-effacement.” Paul knew the grammar of such a sentence from his own experience: I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me.
A station in which he has “no control” over his own weal or woe. The Qur’án of Muḥammad at the battle of Badr: thou threwest not when thou didst throw, but Allah threw.

“I am moved to proclaim … ‘verily I am God!’; and when I consider my own self, lo, I find it coarser than clay!” The Sufi Ḥalláj spoke in the first voice and was executed in Baghdad in 922: I am He whom I love, and He whom I love is I. Bahá’u’lláh gives both sentences together. What does the second do to the first?

“Verily I am God!” The Qur’án is severe on exactly such a sentence: they surely disbelieve who say: Lo! Allah is the Messiah, son of Mary. How do the readings’ three stations, and the mirror that “has no Light in itself,” answer a Muslim’s alarm?
“The station of unity and the station of distinction.” The same Gospel that has “I and my Father are one” has: my Father is greater than I.

The Báb describes two stations, one in which all are poor before him and one in which he is a servant. The Qur’án gives Muḥammad the words of the second: say: I am only a mortal like you. My Lord inspireth in me.
And the voice of the first, as Moses heard it and was told to carry it: I AM hath sent me unto you.
The first station spoken in a human voice to a puzzled disciple. Jesus: he that hath seen me hath seen the Father.
The universal Manifestation is “the mirror held before this Sun.” The Letter to the Hebrews: the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person.
The sun appears in the mirror “with all its perfections.” Paul: in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily.
“The reality is the same sun.” The Letter to the Hebrews: Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever.

Three stations: body, rational soul, and “divine appearance and heavenly splendour.” John’s prologue holds the first and third in one sentence: the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, and we beheld his glory.
The human station is real. Luke: Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and man.

“Their bodies perceive things only according to the capacity of the material world.” Jesus admits a limit of knowledge: of that day and that hour knoweth no man, no, not the angels, neither the Son, but the Father.

Three stations, the highest a perfect manifestation of God. The Christian creeds say more than manifestation: the only-begotten of his Father, very God of very God, begotten, not made, being of one substance with the Father. Where exactly do the readings and the creed part, and what is each guarding?

The divine revelators “eat, they sleep, they are sometimes ill.” The objection of Mecca: what aileth this messenger that he eateth food and walketh in the markets? Why is not an angel sent down unto him?
The shortest verse in the Bible belongs to the human station: Jesus wept.
“The capacities of His human body were limited but the strength of His spirit was vast.” Jesus in Gethsemane: the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.
“Jesus Christ had the same two conditions … and man has the same.” The Letter to the Hebrews: in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá comments on this saying. The passage: now is my soul troubled; and what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour: but for this cause came I unto this hour. Father, glorify thy name.
The same two conditions in one prayer: let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt.
Christ was “the medium for the descent of the bounty of God.” John: no man hath seen God at any time; the only begotten Son, he hath declared him.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá is asked about this saying. Matthew’s version: whosoever speaketh a word against the Son of man, it shall be forgiven him: but whosoever speaketh against the Holy Ghost, it shall not be forgiven him.
The mirror “has no Light in itself … thus the Father is in the Son.” Jesus: believe the works: that ye may know, and believe, that the Father is in me, and I in him.
The human station is “the second veil.” Nazareth: is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary? And they were offended at him.
And the divine station is the scandal. Jerusalem: for a good work we stone thee not; but for blasphemy; and because that thou, being a man, makest thyself God.

He sometimes “addresseth His outward form with the tongue of His inward reality.” Ordinary believers know a small version of this, as in the psalm where a man speaks to himself: why art thou cast down, O my soul? hope thou in God.
“When He saith ‘I am the servant of God,’ it is as His saying ‘I am the Beloved of the worlds.’” At the Jordan the one who had come to be baptized like any penitent heard: this is my beloved Son.
Paul on servant and Lord as one person: he took upon him the form of a servant; wherefore God also hath highly exalted him.

Servant and Beloved are one statement. Guru Gobind Singh would allow himself only the first: all who call me the Supreme Being shall fall into the pit of hell. Recognize me as God’s servant only. What in the readings would he approve, and what would he still refuse?

Two stations: “Abstraction,” in which they commune with God, and the station in which they live among people. Mark: rising up a great while before day, he departed into a solitary place, and there prayed. And Simon said, All men seek for thee.
Moses went between the two with a veil: when he spoke with the Lord he took it off, and when he came out to the people he put it on again.
“All Divine Manifestations give up all personal condition.” Paul: he made himself of no reputation.
“All the Prophets … find their existence in Him.” Paul: he is before all things, and by him all things consist.

The Manifestation has “a twofold nature,” physical and “born of the substance of God Himself.” The Upanishads say something that sounds similar of every person: that subtile essence is the Self, and thou art it. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá says man has two conditions as Christ had. What, then, is unique to the Manifestation in these readings?

john-now-is-my-soul-troubled.text: Now is my soul troubled; and what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour: but for this cause came I unto this hour. Father, glorify thy name

matthew-this-is-my-beloved-son.text: And Jesus, when he was baptized, went up straightway out of the water: and, lo, the heavens were opened unto him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove, and lighting upon him: And lo a voice from heaven, saying, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased

quran-they-disbelieve-who-say-allah-is-t.text: They surely disbelieve who say: Lo! Allah is the Messiah, son of Mary. The Messiah (himself) said: O Children of Israel, worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord. Lo! whoso ascribeth partners unto Allah, for him Allah hath forbidden paradise. His abode is the Fire. For evil-doers there will be no helpers.
